channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Immune changes linked to diabetes could guide development of new cancer treatments
item.description: New research in The Journal of Immunology uncovers how high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) and type 1 diabetes (T1D) may protect against certain cancers like melanoma, breast and colon cancer. T1D has been associated with a decreased risk of certain cancers, but the exact reasons why have remained a mystery. New data from studies in mice now show that it could be due to changes in immune cells, called T cells, caused by hyperglycemia.

item.title: Universal immunization of newborns against RSV could significantly reduce infant hospitalizations in EU
item.description: As the season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory diseases approaches, a new report from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) indicates that universal immunization of newborns against RSV could substantially reduce hospitalizations among infants linked to the disease during the winter season.

item.title: Meal delivery apps could be driving us toward unhealthy choices
item.description: New research has revealed how meal delivery apps are steering Australians toward unhealthy food options, prompting calls from experts for government action to reset the balance and make choosing healthy options easier and more affordable.

item.title: Can an AI chatbot help women recognize heart disease?
item.description: HeartBot, created by a team of UC researchers, regularly answers questions from women seeking information on heart disease. The project was led by Yoshimi Fukuoka, Ph.D., RN, FAAN, a nurse scientist and professor at UC San Francisco's School of Nursing. The goal was to study whether having a heart-health chatbot on their phone would increase study participants' awareness of heart disease risks and recognition of heart attack symptoms so they would seek medical help when necessary.

item.title: Recommendations developed for management of hidradenitis suppurativa
item.description: Evidence-based recommendations are presented for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) in guidelines of care issued by the American Academy of Dermatology and the Hidradenitis Suppurativa Foundation and published online Oct. 20 in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology.

item.title: Video decision aid increases advance care planning in seniors with chronic kidney disease
item.description: Among older adults with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), a video decision aid increases advance care planning (ACP) documentation in the electronic health record, according to a study published in JAMA Internal Medicine to coincide with Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

item.title: Achilles injections show no meaningful benefit over sham treatment
item.description: Commonly used injections for Achilles tendinopathy—pain, stiffness and swelling in the Achilles tendon—offer no meaningful clinical advantage over placebo (sham) treatment, finds a clinical trial published by The BMJ.

item.title: Corridor care is hiding the true scale of the NHS hospital crisis
item.description: The label "corridor care" is hiding the true scale of the NHS hospital crisis, warns a senior doctor in The BMJ today.

item.title: Measles outbreak that contributed to Canada losing elimination status highlights risks from persistent immunity gaps
item.description: The outbreak that contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025 was concentrated in historically undervaccinated communities with close social networks across Canada, the U.S., Mexico and beyond, creating opportunities for cross-border transmission, concludes a study published by The BMJ.

item.title: Wider surgical margins may not mean better cancer control
item.description: It's a question that surgeons often face: How much surrounding healthy tissue should they take out when removing a patient's cancer to be sure it is fully eliminated? Removing more can sacrifice nearby nerves, blood vessels, tendons and even joints, with lasting effects on quality of life.

item.title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
item.description: At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.

item.title: Mutated immune cells raise red flags in lupus
item.description: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) have discovered that patients with lupus have unusual mutations that may turn their bodies into battlegrounds.

item.title: Smarter CAR-T cells could beat a deadly pediatric brain cancer
item.description: Scientists at UC San Francisco have engineered CAR-T cells that stay dormant until they reach the brain, where they switch on and destroy tumor cells. In mice, these CAR-T cells were able to clear diffuse midline glioma (DMG), a lethal form of childhood brain cancer that integrates into healthy tissue. The cells also had staying power. When scientists introduced another round of cancer several weeks later, the cells were still able to fight.

item.title: CDC names the 4 most dangerous superbugs in the US
item.description: Superbugs cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year.

item.title: Large-scale genetic study on Alzheimer's identifies new DNA risks
item.description: A large-scale international study offers new insights for understanding Alzheimer's disease and developing future treatments. The University of Exeter–led PROTECT study was part of the research, led by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and published in Nature, which sheds clearer light on the role of immune cells within the brain, as well as several specific neuronal cell types.

item.title: Biological mechanism underlying Huntington's disease may be more widespread in the brain than previously thought
item.description: In 2025, a team of scientists revealed some unexpected findings about how the inherited DNA repeat associated with Huntington's disease causes the illness—by slowly expanding throughout a person's life, then becoming toxic after enlarging to several times its original length. The findings were in a specific brain region, the striatum, but it wasn't clear if the same process was directly causing the harm in other parts of the brain affected by the disease.

item.title: How sex-based biology shapes the brain's response to injury
item.description: Injury-induced stress cascades through the body by activating immune responses, shifting energy away from less urgent concerns to prioritize healing. In traumatic brain injury, or TBI, the brain—home to the signaling hubs that manage those safety processes—is the site of the incident.

item.title: Deep brain stimulation in patients with epilepsy produces measurable response within minutes, study finds
item.description: Mayo Clinic researchers have detected measurable changes in the brain within 18 minutes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in people with drug-resistant epilepsy, a finding that could eventually help clinicians personalize treatment without waiting months to determine whether stimulation settings are effective. The study was recently published in iScience.

item.title: New microscopy platform enables imaging of neuronal activity at single-cell resolution at unprecedented tissue depth
item.description: As light travels deeper into the brain, it scatters. Three-photon microscopy, the current state of the art, reduces the resulting background fluorescence and can, in principle, image much deeper than earlier techniques—but to do that, it uses average laser power limits that cause overheating and damage living tissue.

item.title: Living near water-pollution sources associated with rare brain disorder
item.description: People who live near industrial facilities that pollute the water supply may be more likely to develop a rare movement disorder called progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), according to a study published in Neurology.

item.title: Tiny corneal bumps reveal potential path toward treating severe vision loss
item.description: University of Waterloo researchers have discovered how tiny bumps inside the eye contribute to Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), an eye disease that can cause severe vision loss. With donated corneas in short supply worldwide, the finding could lead to alternative treatment strategies and reduce the need for corneal transplants in some patients.

item.title: Lab-on-a-chip predicts which cancer treatments may work for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia
item.description: More than 120,000 people in the U.S. are living with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and 6,000 new cases are diagnosed each year. Of those, more than 3,500 will be in children. Responsible for 75% of all pediatric leukemia diagnoses, ALL is a rapid-onset blood cancer, preventing the body from producing mature, infection-fighting white blood cells, sometimes within a matter of months.

item.title: Your bottom shape doesn't reveal your estrogen levels—despite what social media says
item.description: The shape of your bottom cannot tell you anything about your hormones, whatever recent social media posts claim. Determining hormone levels requires appropriate laboratory testing; buttock shape is not a reliable indicator.

item.title: Combining targeted therapies significantly boosted survival in kidney cancer study
item.description: Results of a phase 1/2 trial led by Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center show that combining the targeted therapies bevacizumab (Avastin) and pazopanib (Votrient) significantly extends both progression-free and overall survival in patients with the most common type of kidney cancer. Saby George, M.D., FACP, professor of oncology in the Department of Medicine, is principal investigator of the trial and first author of the study, newly published in The Lancet Oncology.

item.title: Aging people with autism more likely to have Parkinson's disease symptoms
item.description: Older people with autism are more likely to develop symptoms of Parkinson's disease, a new study says.

item.title: Diabetes medication may lower heart attack and stroke risk by curbing platelet overactivation
item.description: For millions living with type 2 diabetes, heart disease remains one of the greatest threats to their health.

item.title: Snake-inspired soft robot could help doctors diagnose and treat small intestine disorders
item.description: Disorders of the small intestine are often difficult to diagnose and treat. More than 20 feet (6.1 meters) long, an inch (2.5 centimeters) in diameter and located deep within the body, this organ is harder to access than other parts of the digestive tract, such as the colon or stomach.

item.title: Health coverage more strongly associated with income than world region
item.description: Higher levels of human development are associated with better universal health coverage worldwide, and disparities in coverage between income groups are generally larger than disparities between world regions. Those are two of the conclusions of a new study published this week in the journal PLOS Global Public Health by Akira Hayasaka of Yokohama City University, Japan, Yasuhiro Nakanishi of the National Institute of Public Health, Japan, and colleagues.

item.title: People in tune with their bodies pay a lower health price for politics, without switching off
item.description: A study of more than 2,000 Americans across two elections found that people who notice and trust their body's signals reported fewer physical, emotional, behavioral and social costs from politics, and were more politically engaged.

item.title: Restoring an amino acid can diminish age-related inflammation
item.description: Sustained low-level inflammation is a hallmark of the aging process. The accumulating damage persistently activates the innate immune system—the body's first line of defense—leading to what is known as inflammaging, functional decline and chronic diseases of old age.
